stories.headline: Astros frustrated by boos from sparse crowd during wild-card opener
stories.summary: The crowd at Daikin Park was surprisingly sparse as the Astros -- baseball's first division winner with a .500 or worse record -- opened their Wild Card Series with a 6-3 loss to the White Sox on Tuesday.
stories.body:
HOUSTON -- The crowd at Daikin Park was surprisingly sparse as the Houston Astros -- baseball's first division winner with a .500 or worse record -- opened their wild-card series with a 6-3 loss to the Chicago White Sox on Tuesday.

Large swaths of seats, especially in the upper deck, sat empty while right-hander AJ Blubaugh delivered the game's first pitch at 4:10 p.m. The bottom two levels were much fuller than the upper deck, but many seats in the lower two decks were also empty.

The announced attendance was 34,011, in a park with a capacity of 40,963.

All those empty seats are a rare sight in a stadium that is normally packed for the postseason. And some of the fans that did show up weren't too happy with the performance of the home team with boos raining down on the Astros in the first and second innings as they fell behind 3-0.

"It's extremely frustrating as a home player," first baseman Christian Walker told The Athletic. "We're here, playing at home; we need cheers. We need energy. We don't need boos. What purpose does that serve in that moment? Whatever fans are feeling, we're feeling it tenfold. We're the ones out there. We're the ones in the fight. We worked our butts off this whole season to put ourselves in this spot, and for guys to get booed, it's frustrating."

Reliever Bennett Sousa was subjected to some boos after spiking two breaking pitches in the seventh inning.

"This team has laid a lot on the line to be in this position to give the fans a playoff game -- a playoff series," Sousa told The Athletic. "We want their support."

Major League Baseball has previously had trouble filling stadiums for some afternoon games in the wild-card round. When Cleveland hosted Detroit last year, the series opener started at 1:08 p.m. with 26,186 in attendance. All three games in that series were played in front of fewer than 30,000 fans. The Tampa Bay Rays drew just 19,704 for an ALWCS opener against Texas in 2023 that started at 3:08 p.m., the lowest attendance for a non-COVID MLB postseason game since the 1919 World Series.

Houston returned to the playoffs after missing out last year despite finishing 81-81. It's the first time a team made the postseason without a winning record in a non-shortened season.

The Astros averaged 30,519 fans per game during the regular season, which ranked 14th in the majors.

Houston fought through an injury-plagued season to reach the playoffs for the ninth time in 10 years. The Astros reached the American League Championship Series seven straight times from 2017-23 and advanced to the World Series four times, winning championships in 2017 and 2022.

stories.headline: Sources: Ravens starting center Jovaughn Gwyn out for 2-3 months
stories.summary: Ravens starting center Jovaughn Gwyn is expected to miss two to three months with a fractured fibula that will likely require surgery, a source told ESPN.
stories.body:
OWINGS MILLS, Md. -- Baltimore Ravens starting center Jovaughn Gwyn is expected to miss two to three months with a fractured fibula that will likely require surgery, a source told ESPN's Jeremy Fowler on Wednesday.

Gwyn was carted off the field during the Ravens' 34-31 win over the Dallas Cowboys in the NFL's first game in Rio de Janeiro.

With backup center Ethan Pocic (knee) also injured, Ravens coach Jesse Minter said Monday that rookie first-round pick Olaivavega Ioane is preparing to make his first start at center for Sunday's game against the Tennessee Titans. Ioane, the No. 14 pick in this year's draft, has started the first three games of the season at right guard.

The Ravens have started to look for offensive line help, working out centers Graham Glasgow and Kingsley Eguakun along with guard Kyle Hergel on Tuesday.

Gwyn, 27, was a starter for the first time in his four-year career when he beat out Pocic for the job in training camp. A seventh-round pick in 2023, he had played his first three seasons as a reserve with the Atlanta Falcons.

Gwyn's injury is the latest setback for the Ravens in their attempt to replace Tyler Linderbaum, a three-time Pro Bowler who became the NFL's highest-paid center when he signed a three-year, $81 million contract with the Las Vegas Raiders in March. Danny Pinter suffered a season-ending knee injury in August after it appeared he was going to win Baltimore's starting center job.

stories.headline: Does Man City's guilty verdict impact Pep Guardiola's legacy as an all-time coaching great?
stories.summary: Pep Guardiola won 16 major honors as Man City manager. They all now count for nothing after the Premier League found the club guilty of systematically breaking financial rules.
stories.body:
Pep Guardiola won 16 major honors during his 10-year reign as Manchester City manager before he left in the summer. They all now count for nothing.

Under Guardiola, City won a Champions League-Premier League-FA Cup treble. They became the only club in English history to win four successive league titles. They were the first team to achieve a domestic treble, and the only side to win the title by amassing 100 points. All of it was built on a false premise.

To borrow a phrase from the Premier League statement that condemned the club's "systematic rule-breaking for almost a decade" following an independent commission's finding that City were guilty of more than 100 breaches of rules between 2009-2018, it was all a "sham."

- Marcotti: Hard to see how City recover from extraordinary guilty verdict

- Dawson: Man City's guilt the talk of the town around English soccer

- Watch: Full reaction to 'the biggest sporting cheating scandal ever'

The egregious actions of City's owners -- Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed al Nahyan's Abu Dhabi United Group (ADUG) -- and executives has destroyed the reputation of a 146-year-old club. City have said they will appeal the verdict, and they maintain they are innocent, but Guardiola cannot escape the damage caused by a prolonged and systematic program of financial deception because much of it was done for his benefit.

Abu Dhabi built a club and a team fit for Guardiola, but it was a construction built by ill-gotten gains. The advantages Guardiola had at his disposal are now proven to have been unfair. As former Manchester United captain Roy Keane said this week: "They [City] won it on the pitch because cheating was going on."

Financial mismanagement, chicanery, deception -- whatever you want to call it, the foundations of Guardiola's City empire are rooted in the rule-breaking that happened before and during his time as manager, so his record-breaking era at the club is tainted by all of it.

But there are two sides to the Guardiola story at City. The former Barcelona and Bayern Munich coach arrived at the Etihad in the summer of 2016 having already won six league titles in Catalonia and Bavaria, as well as two Champions Leagues with Barça. His status as the world's preeminent coach was already secure.

Guardiola is a coaching genius, a man whose tactical brilliance built arguably the world's greatest-ever club side at Barcelona. He reinvented the way the game was played, and his influence is now seen at every level of the game.

It's why City's Abu Dhabi hierarchy, led by Sheikh Mansour and club chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak -- who is also CEO of Mubadala, Abu Dhabi's sovereign wealth fund, and holds senior positions within the Abu Dhabi government -- made such strenuous efforts to hire Guardiola in the first place.

The game Guardiola brought to the Etihad only embellished his reputation as the world's greatest coach. Perhaps the best ever. There can be no denying he made his players better and cemented his reputation as a coach that will forever put him in the conversation of master tacticians.

But what about the trophies and the conveyor belt of success? Guardiola's tactical acumen was in-built, but the super-charged squad building at City could only have happened by the club breaking the rules, which they did time after time after time.

Guardiola's City story did not begin on his arrival in July 2016. That was simply the culmination of Abu Dhabi's long-term plan to install him as coach.

The first building blocks were put in place with the hiring of Ferran Soriano as CEO August of 2012 and Txiki Begiristain as director of football two months later. Both men worked closely with Guardiola at Barcelona -- Soriano was Barça vice-president and Begiristain the club's director of football -- so their recruitment by City was all about getting the band back together, with Guardiola the final, dazzling piece of the jigsaw installed four years later.

And here's the thing. The most damning evidence unearthed by the independent commission that considered the Premier League's 115 charges against City was that the club's owners artificially inflated the club's sponsorship revenue by a staggering £830 million ($1.08 billion) between 2009-2018. But when the seasons are broken down individually, the numbers -- the financial doping -- began to grow aggressively from 2012-13 onward.

In Soriano's first season as City CEO the club's owners, in contravention of Premier League financial rules, topped up their commercial income by £105.75 million. In 2013-14, it was £111.5 million extra; and £107.2 million, on top of the real figure of £16 million, in 2014-15.

In the season before Guardiola arrived, that additional off-the-books figure climbed to £120.17 million-- a financial bonus that helped City prepare for Guardiola's arrival with the signings of Kevin De Bruyne (£55 million from Wolfsburg) and Raheem Sterling (£49 million from Liverpool) in the 12 months prior to their new superstar coach taking charge.

Guardiola told Bayern in December 2015 he would be leaving at the end of that season. However, sources have told ESPN that it was made clear to Sterling that Guardiola wanted him at City, despite his move happening a full year before he left Munich for Manchester.

So Guardiola arrived at City in 2016 with a team fit for a king. It was a little like a Formula 1 team hiring the best driver after constructing a car with a bigger engine, better tires and the best aerodynamics -- all in breach of the rules -- and telling him to win, win and win again. And that's what Guardiola did, with continued help from Abu Dhabi's rule-breaking payments -- known as Tagged Sums -- which climbed to £129.59m in Guardiola's first season and then to £134.73 million in 2017-18.

Imagine giving the best coach in the world all that extra money to make his team better? No wonder City dominated to such an extent under Guardiola.

Guardiola has since said -- incorrectly -- that "nobody from the staff, backroom staff or mainly the players and the manager was here" when the rules were broken between 2009-2018. Guardiola and his staff were there in 2016, 2017 and 2018.

The 55-year-old, who left City at the end of last season, also said: "I trust them [City's owners]. I spoke with them and trust how they behave and how they did," when asked about the charges against the club.

Prior to the 2008 Abu Dhabi takeover, City were an English version of Espanyol or 1860 Munich -- a club with a long, unsuccessful history that was overshadowed by much bigger local and national rivals. Only Guardiola knows what he knows and whether he ever questioned how City suddenly became one of the most powerful in the world. A club that was able to grow revenues greater than Real Madrid, Barcelona, Manchester United and Liverpool and one that could attract superstar names including Erling Haaland, De Bruyne, Sergio Agüero and himself as coach.

For a mid-size club with no global fanbase or extensive trophy-winning history to do all of that legitimately through sheer hard work is remarkable, maybe the greatest sporting story of all-time.

But we now know that it was anything but. It was a fairytale story, but a twisted one with a sinister ending, and Guardiola and his teams are inextricably linked to that.

stories.headline: Predictions for every NHL team's finish in 2026-27: Why the Panthers will win the Cup
stories.summary: Some fans will wait to watch all the games this season. Readers of this story won't need to!
stories.body:
As is tradition, I reached out to the general manager of my Stanley Cup champion-in-waiting to let him know what's coming.

Florida Panthers GM Bill Zito's reaction to my pick: "FINALLY!"

I didn't pick the Panthers when they won the Stanley Cup in 2024, because the Edmonton Oilers were supposed to do that. I didn't pick them the following year when Florida won again, because I figured it was the Dallas Stars' turn to win.

So I'm happy someone had the confidence to give the underrated and overlooked Florida Panthers, who have won three conference titles and two Stanley Cups in the last four seasons, their Stanley Cup pick.

I have the Panthers winning hockey's Holy Grail again over the Colorado Avalanche, who channel their frustration from a conference final defeat into a run to the NHL's last round ... only to find the deepest, nastiest and most self-assured team in hockey ready to pounce on another title.

What about the rest of the NHL? Here's my division-by-division breakdown of the projected standings. Playoff teams are bolded. Good luck to all 32 teams. I hope everyone has fun out there.

ATLANTIC DIVISION
Tampa Bay Lightning

Montreal Canadiens

Florida Panthers

Toronto Maple Leafs

Buffalo Sabres

Boston Bruins

Ottawa Senators

Detroit Red Wings

The Tampa Bay Lightning amassed 106 points in a season with several key players missing chunks of time, battling through injuries and, in the case of captain Victor Hedman, off-ice matters. Coach Jon Cooper finally won the Jack Adams Award for keeping this rickety ship sailing straight, with assists from Nikita Kucherov (130 points, winning the Hart Trophy) and Andrei Vasilevskiy (39 wins, capturing the Vezina Trophy).

Given the dominance of their top six and a deeper blue line thanks to the addition of new power-play QB John Carlson, it's hard to imagine the Lightning finishing anywhere but near the top of the Atlantic, as long as Vasilevskiy holds up his end of the bargain. But then comes the hard part: Getting out of the first round, something they haven't done since winning their second of back-to-back Cups in 2021. If that happens again, is it time for some changes?

The Canadiens were the last Canadian team to win the Stanley Cup in 1993 and are poised to become the next one to lift it. GM Kent Hughes is really putting the pieces in place, what with Nick Suzuki and Cole Caufield locked into the top line; Ivan Demidov powering the second line; and Phillip Danault centering the third line. The addition of Chris Kreider adds some veteran physicality and leadership to a team that already earned an education in its conference finals loss to Carolina.

It still feels like a team that's a year away from breaking through the conference ceiling. That said, its strong young goaltending and dynamic defenseman Lane Hutson -- my personal pick for the Norris Trophy this season -- might make it ahead of schedule. Montreal is a legit Cup threat.

We all know the Panthers have three dominant forward lines and two championship-caliber defensive pairings. What makes this team special is how these star players approach the game. "Humility" isn't often associated with the Florida Panthers, but it's one of the secret ingredients to their success. There have been team meetings over the years in which players are asked about their individual stats and they can't recall them. No one cares who scores the game-winning goal as long as the game is won -- and the Panthers have the utmost confidence that the guy next to them in the locker room can score that goal.

That's why I think Brady Tkachuk is going to work extremely well with the Panthers. He goes from having the weight on his shoulders and the spotlight in his eyes as the Senators' franchise player to being a gear in a well-run machine in Florida. This isn't to say that Tkachuk can't be "the guy" if needed, just that there's a different comfort and confidence level for a star player to walk into a dressing room already filled with Stanley Cup rings. See also: Mitch Marner in Vegas last season.

Every person around the NHL that I've spoken to about the Panthers echo the same sentiment: a healthy Aleksander Barkov and a rested roster are scary, but can Jacob Markstrom sufficiently replace Sergei Bobrovsky? To that I'd say the Panthers knew Bob might price himself off the roster and had game-planning out potential replacements. Markstrom was vetted and eventually acquired from the Devils. They believe he can be what they need -- and that the team in front is great enough to overcome a potential downgrade in goal to win a third Stanley Cup in four seasons.

After the Maple Leafs acquired Blue Jackets leading goal scorer Kirill Marchenko this week, a former NHL front office executive texted me to say, "You may have to upgrade Toronto" in the standings projections.

The trade that sent Matthew Knies to Columbus for Marchenko doesn't just give Auston Matthews his most talented linemate since Mitch Marner -- although Marchenko doesn't have Marner's defensive chops. It's the clearest indication of GM John Chayka's intention for the roster. Both Marchenko and Knies stand at 6-foot-3, but Knies had about 30 pounds on the newest Leaf. Knies is the player you keep on the roster if your team is specifically designed to take on the likes of the Panthers. Marchenko is the player whom you acquire if you're leaning into skill instead of bulk, a direction Leafs fans have been begging this team to take since the Core 4 ruled the Six.

First overall pick Gavin McKenna fits into that as well, but he also serves a more important purpose: a lottery win that gave the Leafs a sense of future and purpose right as it seemed like the franchise was on the precipice of entering its next phase.

Chayka's aggressive reshaping of the rest of the roster had its "throw all the bottom-six forwards at the wall and see what sticks" chaos, but it wasn't without salient improvements such as Darren Raddysh's addition to the blue line. Enough of those bets will pay off, and the Leafs will return to the postseason.

The Buffalo Sabres making the Stanley Cup playoffs in back-to-back seasons might have previously been seen as a sign of the apocalypse, but Buffalo will return to the party as a wild card.

The crushing weight of the playoff drought has been lifted, but the bigger psychological development is a collection of young players getting playoff experience and the confidence that comes with it. Josh Doan, Jack Quinn, Noah Ostlund and especially Zach Benson are all progressing nicely and ready for greater responsibilities. Throw in rookie wild cards such as Konsta Helenius and Jiri Kulich, and the Sabres are as fueled by youthful exuberance as they are by stars such as Tage Thompson and Rasmus Dahlin.

David Pastrnak is going to score 100 points, Jeremy Swayman is going to make a bunch of saves, and Charlie McAvoy is going to move the puck and throw the body. The Boston Bruins have won with a holy hockey trinity before -- Bergeron, Chara and Rask, hallowed be thy names -- but usually with a supporting cast that has fewer question marks than the current incarnation of the Bruins.

It's hard to imagine Pavel Zacha and Morgan Geekie running it back after career years, or the team's prospects such as James Hagens and Fraser Minten leveling up to the point of moving the needle.

I do like the addition of JJ Peterka, whose ill-fitting time in Utah ended after one season. But there's just not enough offense for me to depend on after Pasta.

The Ottawa Senators naming Quebecois Thomas Chabot as their captain was the most obvious thing in the history of obvious things. Jake Sanderson is younger, better, signed for longer and absolutely capable of captaining a team. But he's probably on the Team USA Olympic group chat, and this team plays in Ottawa and just saw previous captain Brady Tkachuk migrate to South Florida.

No matter how fractured things were with Tkachuk after the Olympics, he was one of the Senators' most consistent regular-season performers, with 59 points in 60 games last season. They're not replacing that point production or his snarly intangibles. Getting William Eklund from the Sharks certainly increases the skill level of a team that already has Tim Stutzle and Drake Batherson driving play at the forward spot, but there's not enough pop here to keep up with the rest of the division.

There is, however, an extremely good defensive team under the guidance of coach Travis Green. As Linus Ullmark showed in the playoffs last season, he's still an elite goaltender when locked in. It's not out of the realm of possibility that Ottawa can sneak into the playoffs on the strength of that team defense.

Detroit is a mess. Captain Dylan Larkin requested a trade ... and as punishment Detroit made him continue to play for the Red Wings with fewer responsibilities, taking away the captaincy. They're grinding 23-year-old defenseman Simon Edvinsson in a contract negotiation. Worst of all, the franchise had to finally admit the "Yzerplan" was a failure, as franchise icon Steve Yzerman left the general manager's office after seven playoff-less seasons.

The Red Wings have a few reasons for hope, such as defenseman Moritz Seider, winger Lucas Raymond and a prospect pool that's filling up but without any franchise-level talents.

In the long term, maybe the plan is hoping the Hughes brothers all want to play close to their Michigan roots when Jack is a free agent in 2030. In the short term, there's speculation about who's leaving next after Larkin is dealt, and does his name rhyme with "Alex DeBrincat?"

METROPOLITAN DIVISION
Carolina Hurricanes

New Jersey Devils

Washington Capitals

Philadelphia Flyers

Columbus Blue Jackets

Pittsburgh Penguins

New York Rangers

New York Islanders

Nothing is going to detract from the Hurricanes' hard-fought and well-earned Stanley Cup championship, the prize at the end of an absolutely dominant postseason run. This is essentially the same roster that skated the Cup on Vegas ice: a perfect alchemy of the Hurricanes' defensive hallmarks (in players such as Jaccob Slavin and Jordan Staal) and the offensive spark plugs that powered their championship engine (Nikolaj Ehlers and Logan Stankoven among them).

However ... don't we all want to see Carolina go through their tormentors from South Florida for another shot at the Stanley Cup? To witness the last two champions in a slobber-knocker, especially now that GM Eric Tulsky has built a roster as good as any that the Panthers have faced? Of course we do, and not just for the Southeast Division nostalgia of it all. And given the strengths of both teams, we might get it.

A caveat about the Canes' season: There seems to be a growing sentiment that the Hurricanes are going to eventually solve their Alexander Nikishin problem -- an unsigned restricted free agent defenseman seeking a change in scenery -- by solving the Winnipeg Jets' Connor Hellebuyck problem, likely through a three-way trade of some sort. With due respect to the newly signed Pyotr Kochetkov and playoff legend Brandon Bussi, putting a multitime Vezina winner in a Rod Brind'Amour system behind that blue line is like putting a wall made of adamantium in front of the Hurricanes' net.

Stop me if you've heard this one before: The New Jersey Devils' success will hinge on the health of star center Jack Hughes and the quality of their goaltending. Rinse, repeat.

They went 34-24-3 with the Olympic hero on the ice last season and 8-13-0 without him. Their goaltending was 21st in the NHL in save percentage, thanks to the .903 that Jake Allen put up in 37 games. Jacob Markstrom was traded to Florida, which means the crease belongs to Allen and Nico Daws -- with Mikhail Yegorov gestating at Boston University.

New GM Sunny Mehta didn't take gargantuan swings in the offseason. (Potential Quinn Hughes trade pending.) Rather, he added some sorely needed scoring depth so the Devils might withstand the absence of Jack Hughes better than they have in previous seasons. Anthony Mantha, Luke Evangelista, Evan Rodrigues and Amadeus Lombardi join a forward pool that also includes Arseny Gritsyuk, who showed flashes of brilliance last season.

The Washington Capitals have a tantalizingly high ceiling this season. Like the Panthers and Hurricanes, every line brings something to the table. I love their mix of established veterans and young impact players such as Ilya Protas and Cole Hutson. I love that they can win a match of skills or one game pummeling one another in the corners. Logan Thompson is now overdue to win the Vezina Trophy, giving them goaltending on which they can build a contender.

What's holding me back from anointing the Capitals as conference champions, because the potential is there? Their Stanley Cup championship was won with John Carlson, Matt Niskanen, Dmitry Orlov and Brooks Orpik logging the most ice time. I don't see that presence or pedigree within their current defense corps. That could change with a deadline deal or two, but that's the only glaring concern on an otherwise stout roster. Alex Ovechkin's last NHL season -- we think? -- is going to be a lengthy one.

The rest of this division you could basically pick out of a hat and have a decent chance of getting the order right. That's not to say the Metro Division's other five teams are beyond my power of prognostication, but that there's so little daylight between them that any of them could be fourth and any of them could be eighth and none of it would be surprising.

Take the Philadelphia Flyers, who ended a five-season playoff drought and won a playoff round last season. There's at least a little fear around the team that there's going to be a step back before there's a leap forward with a young but very talented roster.

Just a little regression from their forward group or goalie Dan Vladar could turn a three-points playoff bubble cushion into a postseason miss.

In fact, one could argue that the Flyers wouldn't have made the playoffs had the Columbus Blue Jackets not epically face-planted with two wins in their last 11 games last season. The biggest question facing Columbus is what, if any, impact the turbulent offseason is going to have on the team. Norris winner Zach Werenski reportedly indicated he wasn't signing another contract with the Blue Jackets, vetoed a trade to the Stars and spent the next two months on a PR campaign to smooth things over with the fanbase.

Kirill Marchenko, their leading goal scorer for three seasons, declared he wanted out and was traded to Toronto for a package centered around Matthew Knies.

Now that the noise has quieted, are the Blue Jackets a playoff team? Potentially, if they look as good as they looked for much of Rick Bowness' time as head coach last season. Adam Fantilli is just getting started and leads a solid trio of centers with Sean Monahan and Charlie Coyle. They're going to have to get goal scoring from veteran wingers such as Valeri Nichushkin, imported from Colorado, and Conor Garland. They obviously also need young forwards Cole Sillinger and Kent Johnson to progress as Fantilli has.

The defense is in good hands with Werenski, Ivan Provorov and the underrated Denton Mateychuk. One assumed Jet Greaves' breakout season in goal wasn't a fluke. Like the Flyers, they're right on the cusp.

The Pittsburgh Penguins were an unlikely playoff team last season after they ended up last in the Metro in most projections. Can Sidney Crosby and Evgeni Malkin conjure another postseason party in their sunset years? That depends on three factors:

1. How much second-year coach Dan Muse can tease out of the team's supporting cast, after a masterful job last season.

2. Whether Erik Karlsson, finally in the last year of his contract, has another remarkable season in him after 66 points in 75 games, finishing ninth for the Norris.

3. How quickly rookie goalie Sergei Murashov can ascend to the starter's role and whether his play is good enough to separate the Penguins from the Metro pack.

I think the improvement of the rest of the division keeps the Penguins out. Which is a bummer, because I want all the Sidney Crosby in championship tournament spotlights I can get, as the clock ticks.

Full disclosure: An early draft of these projections had the New York Rangers as a wild-card team, even as they announced a "retool" earlier this season. Retool they have, adding Marcus Pettersson and Sean Durzi to round out a pretty good group on the back end led by the resurgent Adam Fox and solidified by Igor Shesterkin, one of the best goalies on the planet.

They also traded for Vegas winger Pavel Dorofeyev and handed him a seven-year deal worth $11 million annually against the salary cap. If he pops for another 30-plus goal season, the Rangers' ceiling is a bit higher in the standings. If he doesn't, because neither Jack Eichel or Mitch Marner is on the Rangers, then the climb becomes a bit steep. His two goals over the final nine playoff games last postseason gave me pause.

Dorofeyev isn't the only player whose performance could level this group up. If Gabe Perreault doubles his points, Will Cuylle bounces back from a regression year and Alexis Lafrenière finally answers "When will Alexis Lafrenière become a star?" with "Right now, baby," the Rangers could end up in the postseason. If not, the "retool" continues."

Someone who doesn't miss the playoffs often is New York Islanders coach Pete DeBoer, who took over with four games left last season. Not counting his cameo appearance last season and when he was fired by the Sharks after 33 games, DeBoer's teams have made the playoffs in nine of 10 seasons.

Alas, those Sharks and Knights and Stars teams were much more talented than this current group on the Island, despite the presence of rookie of the year defenseman and franchise touchstone Matthew Schaefer, as well as goalie Ilya Sorokin. It feels like a franchise stuck between previous iterations of the team and whatever the Islanders will look like in the Schaefer era.

CENTRAL DIVISION
Colorado Avalanche

Dallas Stars

Minnesota Wild

Utah Mammoth

St. Louis Blues

Nashville Predators

Winnipeg Jets

Chicago Blackhawks

Injuries to Cale Makar and Nathan MacKinnon gave the Colorado Avalanche plausible deniability for losing in the 2026 Western Conference finals, but let's face it: They weren't playing well enough at 5-on-5 to win the Stanley Cup anyway. MacKinnon and Brock Nelson had zero goals in 13 games at evens; Martin Necas and Artturi Lehkonen had one each. Over the last two rounds, Mackenzie Blackwood (.890) and Scott Wedgewood (.874) were a faint echo of their regular-season success.

After having the league's best record in the regular season, those diminishing returns must make the Avalanche angry -- and I like the Avalanche when they're angry.

Brent Burns trimmed his beard. That's how you know it's serious.

They were the best offensive (3.63 goals per game) and defensive team (2.40 goals against per game) last season. I don't expect the Lumber Yard (Blackwood and Wedgewood) to lead the league in save percentage again, but I do think Blackwood becoming the de facto starter will help slow that regression to the mean. MacKinnon and Makar drive play like few others can. The supporting cast took a little hit in the offseason, but I love the Jaden Schwartz addition and look forward to a full season of Nazem Kadri back in familiar stomping grounds.

Plus, I have unending faith in newly reestablished GM Joe Sakic to aggressively improve the team if necessary ... provided opposing GMs are dumb enough to pick up the phone.

Only one team had a better regular-season points percentage than the Avalanche over the last three seasons (.673), and that's the Dallas Stars.

They enter the season with Jason Robertson, the 45-goal scorer who sweated out a contentious contract standoff for a one-year deal ($12 million AAV) that walks him up to unrestricted free agency, and with a healthy Tyler Seguin, who looked incredible last season before (another) injury derailed him.

They enter this season without now Nashville center Mavrik Bourque, a rising star turned cap casualty who had 20 goals last season, and without current Columbus defenseman Zach Werenski, who vetoed a trade to Dallas in the offseason. But the Werenski ordeal is another example of GM Jim Nill trying to take the huge swing when the opportunity presents itself -- like when he acquired Mikko Rantanen, who had 77 points in 64 games last season to help drive the offense.

But the reason the Stars aren't the Avalanche is the scoring depth beyond Robertson, Rantanen and Wyatt Johnston. Dallas was ninth in goals per game (3.33) and 21st in expected goals at 5-on-5 last season. The slow leak of middle-six scoring talent -- Bourque, Logan Stankoven, Mason Marchment and Mikael Granlund, to name a few -- and the decline of players such as Matt Duchene is catching up with the Stars. But they're still the second-best team in the division, because they have discernible center depth, unlike the third-best team in the division.

The Minnesota Wild remain the NHL's most decadent artisan doughnut: gourmet ingredients on the outside and nothing in the middle.

The Wild have a tenacious collection of wingers led by goal-scoring stars Kirill Kaprizov and Matt Boldy; they have a stout blue line, toplined by Norris winner Quinn Hughes and the rock-solid Brock Faber (whenever he returns from injury); and they have one of the best goalie tandems in the NHL with Filip Gustavsson and Jesper "The Wall" Wallstedt. And their No. 1 center is Joel Eriksson Ek.

What makes Minnesota so intriguing is the potential variance in its season. If GM Bill Guerin persuades the team from Hockeytown to trade Dylan Larkin, a close friend of fellow Olympian Quinn Hughes, to the State of Hockey, then that hole at center gets much smaller and the Wild's Stanley Cup odds get much better.

Then again, if it becomes apparent that all this dillydallying by Hughes about a contract extension just means he's going to bolt for his brothers' condo in New Jersey next summer, that could dramatically alter Guerin's plans. Keep him for a Cup run or get something before he skates away? That's why they pay Billy the big bucks.

Speaking of variance: How much higher can the Utah Mammoth climb above their 92 points last season if Dylan Guenther and Logan Cooley reach the next tier of their stardom? Guenther, 23, popped for 40 goals last season. Cooley, 22, might have joined him were it not for an injury that limited him to 54 games, as he scored 24 times.

GM Bill Armstrong did the thing that young contending teams do and imported some veteran leadership this offseason in Swiss Army knife forward Vincent Trocheck from the Rangers and Islanders captain Anders Lee. They form a nice experienced core with returning forwards Clayton Keller and Nick Schmaltz, who were a stabilizing force last season.

We know they can score. The Mammoth's success ultimately comes down to their defense corps -- which will be without promising Maveric Lamoureux for at least four months -- and the goaltending tandem of the tireless Karel Vejmelka and former Red Wings prospect Sebastian Cossa. Unless, of course, the Jets could be convinced to send Connor Hellebuyck to Salt Lake City.

The St. Louis Blues are one of my surprise teams this season. They sucked me in with their last 25 games, posting a .740 points percentage with the best goals-against average (2.16) in the league and a top-10 offense.

That's what happens when you turn your crease over to Joel Hofer, who went 12-2-2 in 16 starts to Jordan Binnington's nine appearances (5-3-1). Hofer had a .933 save percentage in that stretch. I don't think that was an aberration -- he's a goalie on the rise. Binnington, meanwhile, is in the last year of his contract. Maybe he ups his game for his next deal. Maybe he's wearing another uniform by the trade deadline.

I'm also confident that the trio of Dylan Holloway, Robert Thomas and Jimmy Snuggerud fuels this team's playoff journey. They produced 5.7 goals and allowed 1.4 goals against per 60 minutes. That's a preposterous 80.1% goals share at 5-on-5. If they can stay healthy -- a legit concern with Thomas and Holloway -- they have the potential to be the best line in the conference and carry this team offensively. Although it would be nice if players such as Jake Neighbours, Dalibor Dvorsky and the newly acquired Mason McTavish help shoulder that goal-scoring load.

Squint hard enough at the Nashville Predators, and this collection of Barry Trotz acquisitions and Chris MacFarland augmentations looks like a playoff team.

Steven Stamkos and Ryan O'Reilly clicked, leading to Stammer's 42-goal season. Filip Forsberg had 40 goals of his own, and I'm excited to see how he works with young winger Matthew Wood. They could go a solid three lines deep.

It's the blue line beyond Roman Josi's top paring, as well as goalie Juuse Saros's frustrating decline, that's like an anchor dragging back their momentum. That said, even if this is coach Andrew Brunette's final season, it should be a fun ride.

It's been a lot less fun these days in Winnipeg. The Jets watched their franchise goalie Connor Hellebuyck peace out with a trade demand, suspending the multiple-time Vezina winner for not reporting to camp. Last season wasn't his greatest, but he's still a goalie with a .927 save percentage and a 1.98 goals-against average at 5-on-5 over his last 180 games. Due respect to Stuart Skinner, but there's no replacing that.

There's apparently also no replacing Nikolaj Ehlers. The winger's departure as a free agent in 2025, combined with several injuries on last year's roster, saw the Jets' offense plummet from 3.35 to 2.79 goals per game. Without the usual Hellebuyck safety net in a down year, that led to a staggering 34-point drop in the standings.

There's still a nice core here with Mark Scheifele, Kyle Connor and Josh Morrissey. They could be better than expected if young players such as Viggo Bjorck, Isak Rosen and Brad Lambert level up, and if Cole Perfetti reverses his regression. But no Helly, no playoffs, no matter what comes back the other way in his eventual trade.

How far the Jets slide down the standings will determine whether or not the Chicago Blackhawks finish last in the Central for a fifth straight season.

In a major leap forward for the franchise, there are now multiple reasons to watch Chicago this season beyond the continuing offensive adventures of Connor Bedard. Center Anton Frondell (19) could challenge for the Calder. Center Frank Nazar (22) is maturing nicely into a point-producing pivot. Can defenseman Bowen Byram prove worthy of his six-year deal with an elephantine $12.5 million cap hit? Will Patrick Kane be something more than a nostalgia play?

The Blackhawks might not win much else this season, but they've recaptured our attention.

PACIFIC DIVISION
Edmonton Oilers

Vegas Golden Knights

San Jose Sharks

Anaheim Ducks

Los Angeles Kings

Seattle Kraken

Vancouver Canucks

Calgary Flames

I guess I see things differently than Connor McDavid. I thought what has held the Edmonton Oilers back from winning the Stanley Cup are factors like not having a good bottom six, not having six good defensemen, and a cursed goaltending situation that left Edmonton unclear about who would actually start an elimination game in the Final.

Connor obviously felt the problem was the Oilers not having an NHL coaching pariah with an inflated legacy using his sports psychology degree to squeeze another percent of effort out of the best player in the world, all while fighting the urge to invade his players' personal electronic devices.

However this Mike Babcock hiring turns out -- I know it's subtle, but I'm skeptical -- the quintet of McDavid, Leon Draisaitl, Zach Hyman, Ryan Nugent-Hopkins and Evan Bouchard will drive this team to its first division title since 1987, which is a truly wild gap of titles given the team's successful history.

Then the real questions can start being answered, especially the one about their goaltending: Can the three-headed monster of Tristan Jarry, Devon Levi and Stanley Cup champ Frederik Andersen finally give McDavid the championship quality netminding he's lacked in Edmonton?

The Vegas Golden Knights' reign of dominance is now 10 years old, having won six division titles, three conference titles and the Stanley Cup. The coaches during that reign: Gerard Gallant, Pete DeBoer, Bruce Cassidy and John Tortorella. All experienced, all accomplished and three of them with Jack Adams Awards. Tortorella took over the Golden Knights with eight games left in the regular season and led them to the Cup Final. He wanted to come back. But GM Kelly McCrimmon told him that Ryan Craig is his guy.

Boy, is he. Craig played for McCrimmon's beloved Brandon Wheat Kings. He joined the Golden Knights as an assistant coach in their inaugural season before taking over their AHL club for the past three seasons -- missing the playoffs twice, for what it's worth. He's been primed to take over this gig for the entirety of the team's existence, handpicked by his boss to replace a coach who had just led them to within two wins of a championship. (That's nothing to say for how good Mitch Marner played under Tortorella, too.)

The Golden Knights collect stars like they're playing a round of "Mario Party," which is why they're going to finish first or second in the Pacific again. But for the first time in their short history, they don't begin the season with a star behind the bench. No pressure, Ryan Craig. You're just a handpicked guy seeking to meet the highest standard of excellence for any NHL team in the last decade.

Please recall that Sidney Crosby played for the Stanley Cup in his third season. I'm not willing to go quite that far with his heir apparent, but I do have Macklin Celebrini winning the Rocket Richard, the Hart Trophy and Lululemon curator of the year in leading the San Jose Sharks back to the playoffs for the first time since 2019.

He is surrounded by a roster filled with young potential stars such as Will Smith (nearly there), Michael Misa, Sam Dickinson and Ivar Stenberg, their latest stroke of draft lottery luck.

But GM Mike Grier has been slowly building a truculent supporting cast in the punishing Western Conference, from his Kiefer Sherwood pickup last season to adding Jacob Trouba to an improved blue line that also now includes Darnell Nurse. You'd like a little more in goal from Alex Nedeljkovic and especially Yaroslav Askarov, who was an atrocious minus-19 goals saved above expected last season, and maybe the new vets on the back end help that out.

The Anaheim Ducks lost Trouba from their back end last season. Olen Zellweger is now a Sabre. Radko Gudas is back in Florida. John Carlson, added at the deadline, is in Tampa. None of them were sufficiently replaced on the fifth-worst team in expected goals against (5-on-5) in the league last season.

Granted, GM Pat Verbeek had to deal with his star center Leo Carlsson signing a $90 million offer sheet from the Flyers, matching it, and then figuring out how much more he had to pay leading scorer Cutter Gauthier ... because of Leo Carlsson signing a $90 million offer sheet from the Flyers. Maybe he was too busy to build on this team's playoff round victory last season, because this roster looks primed for a dip.

Having the Los Angeles Kings outside of the playoff picture just seems wrong. They've made the postseason cut five straight times. New coach Peter Laviolette has made the playoffs in his first full season at each of his six previous NHL coaching stops. They're going to have a full season of star winger Artemi Panarin skating up with Quinton Byfield and either Adrian Kempe or Kevin Fiala when healthy. Their back end features master Drew Doughty, his apprentice Brandt Clarke and the steady work of veteran goalie Darcy Kuemper.

What they don't have is a replacement for Anze Kopitar, who never received the appreciation for how much he did for the Kings in his sunset years. Will they have to move Kempe in the middle for depth's sake, further exposing a past-their-prime group of wingers? There's always a possibility of a trade for a center, but the Kings will have to take a number before being served one -- nearly every team wants another scoring center.

There's a chance I'm wrong here and the Kings vacuum up points in a weak division to make the playoff cut again. But their scoring depth and lack of overall team speed concerns me, even under a coach that gets results.

The best thing for the Seattle Kraken this season would be to be terrible, but this franchise continues to exhibit a stubborn inability to suck. They've never had a points percentage under .463 since their inaugural season. They haven't selected in the top four since drafting Shane Wright in 2022, a young center currently best known for being potential trade bait. Coach Lane Lambert has a system that squeezes out enough points to keep the bubble in sight.

Seattle's analytically driven front office continues to make the nice move here and there: Securing Bobby McMann from the Leafs, getting Mackie Samoskevich from Florida and finally unlocking Kaapo Kakko's potential. Assuming a bounce-back from Joey Daccord, their goaltending is quite solid. But the Kraken are once again neither good enough for the playoffs nor bad enough to maximize their draft lottery odds. They are the embodiment of hockey purgatory.

You probably won't find a standings projection that doesn't have the Vancouver Canucks and Calgary Flames in the bottom of the Pacific. I'm buying into the vibe shift in Vancouver, with the Sedin twins running hockey operations above beloved former player and now head coach Manny Malhotra. They have two potentially solid scoring lines anchored by Elias Pettersson and Jake DeBrusk as well as Marco Rossi and Brock Boeser.

It'll be fun to see if Zeev Buium, who like Rossi came over in the Quinn Hughes trade, has another level.

The Canucks should be better than 31st in scoring, which is where they were last season. I'm not sure the Flames will be better than last in the league again, and that's fine. GM Craig Conroy is in the middle of a rebuild that he's handling adeptly.

Unless goaltenders Dustin Wolf and Devin Cooley prevent the bottom from falling out, the Flames should be 8th-of-8 in the Pacific.

stories.headline: WNBA playoffs 2026: How the Mystics and Wings can stay alive
stories.summary: With home-court advantage on their side, Washington and Dallas look to stave off elimination in the first round.
stories.body:
The Indiana Fever kept their season alive. Can the Washington Mystics and Dallas Wings do the same Wednesday?

Both teams missed the WNBA playoffs the past two years but must take advantage of their home courts and win Wednesday to avoid being eliminated in the first round.

The No. 5 seed Mystics host the No. 4 Atlanta Dream (7 p.m. ET, ESPN) and the No. 7 Wings host the No. 2 Golden State Valkyries (9 p.m. ET, ESPN) in Game 2 of their best-of-three series.

In Sunday's playoff openers, the Mystics fell 92-77 at Atlanta, and the Wings lost 104-80 at Golden State. Washington led by five at halftime, but the game turned around with the Dream's huge 29-12 third-quarter surge. The Wings, prepared for the Valkyries' league-best defense, couldn't keep pace with Golden State's 18 3-pointers and franchise-record scoring total.

Sunday was the first playoff experience for five 2025 first-round draft picks: Dallas' Paige Bueckers and Aziaha James, and Washington's Sonia Citron, Kiki Iriafen and Georgia Amoore.

"This is the stage we want to be on," Iriafen said after Sunday's loss. "This is our first time being here. Not that that's an excuse, but now we know what it looks like. We have a taste for it. We'll be better prepared for our game on Wednesday."

The Mystics and Wings go in with the mission of beating the higher seed. Washington defeated Atlanta twice in the regular season, but Dallas lost three times to Golden State. Here's a look at what could determine Wednesday's results.

What must the Mystics do differently?
Voepel: First, cut down on turnovers, which really hurt them in Game 1. The Mystics had 22 turnovers to seven for Atlanta, with the Dream scoring 27 points off the giveaways to only four for the Mystics.

"They're a very physical team; they have good defenders," Citron said of the turnover issue. "We can't let them speed us up. It's kind of on us."

Overall, both teams played aggressive defense, but the Dream had the better of that, especially when they took control in the third quarter.

"I think we just let them get comfortable offensively," Citron said. "In the first half, we did a good job of just making everything hard for them. In that third quarter, we just let some of our discipline slip. Once they get going, it's really hard to stop them."

Washington did, though, in two out of three games in the regular season, beating the Dream 81-76 on July 2 and 79-74 on Aug. 7. Both games were at Washington, as opposed to the Mystics' 109-77 loss at Atlanta on June 6.

Coach Sydney Johnson said overall, the Mystics -- most of whom were appearing in their first playoff game -- performed pretty well. But that's not enough in the postseason.

"There's an elevated level of play in the playoffs," Johnson said. "I was really proud of how we met that. But we probably met it instead of initiating it in the third and fourth quarters."

What must the Wings do differently?
Andrews: The Wings need more from everyone not named Paige Bueckers. She had a historic night in her playoff debut, becoming the first player in WNBA history to shoot at least 90% from the field and score 20 points or more in her first postseason game. But no one else stepped up to help her. At halftime, Dallas' bench was scoreless and none of the other three players who had scored for the Wings had over six points. Yes, by the end of the game the Wings' second unit was outscored by only four points, but by then the game was decided.

"The score should not dictate your effort," Wings coach Jose Fernandez said after the game.

Jessica Shepard, a candidate for Most Improved Player, was held scoreless. The Valkyries have done a good job at keeping Shepard quiet in some of their previous matchups this season, but she still found other ways to influence the game. In Game 1, she lacked her usual impact on the boards and as a facilitator, finishing with three rebounds, three assists and three turnovers. Arike Ogunbowale and Awak Kuier will also need to produce more.

Bueckers said the Wings' lackluster offensive night also impacted their defense, something they need to change if they want to extend the series.

"We've been a team that has a bad habit of letting made or missed shots dictate how hard we play on the defensive end," Bueckers said. "This is the playoffs, so it's really unacceptable."

What's at stake for the Dream and the Valkyries?
Voepel: Atlanta last made the semifinals in 2018, then missed the playoffs the next four seasons. The Dream returned to the playoffs in 2023 behind Rhyne Howard, the 2022 No. 1 pick, and Allisha Gray, who came to Atlanta that year in a trade from Dallas. They've been the Dream's scoring leaders in all four of their seasons together in Atlanta. But first-round playoff exits the past three years have been a disappointment.

The Dream were swept by Dallas in 2023 and by New York in 2024. Last season against Indiana, the Dream won their first-round opener at home, then lost the next two games and the series.

"The next game is going to be hard," Howard said of Wednesday's matchup in Washington. "They're going to want to come out with more aggression. What we did in the first half, we can't have happen again."

The Valkyries, meanwhile, are in only their second season of existence, but they are ahead of schedule for the average expansion team in pro sports. Last season, as the No. 8 seed, they were swept by Minnesota in the first round.

After shutting down the Wings' inside game Sunday, the Valkyries know that will probably be a point of emphasis for Dallas to greatly improve on in Game 2. And as good as Golden State's offense looked in Game 1, the Valkyries generally do not want high-scoring battles. If they win and close out the series, it might be a very different game than the opener.

Andrews: Before the Valkyries even left the court in Game 1, coach Natalie Nakase's staff was already talking strategy for Game 2. They know the Wings will make adjustments, and they also can't necessarily expect them to have as historic of a shooting night in Game 2. But the Valkyries feel extremely confident.

Golden State's defensive mindset has been one of the most unshakable identities in the WNBA this season, and that's not changing now. Even after Bueckers scored 21 points on 9-of-10 shooting, the Valkyries were pleased with their approach.

"She's an excellent player, one of the best in the league," Christyn Williams said. "As long as I can make [her shots] hard, where she has to really work for them, she will get tired. That's the goal. She's going to get them, but how can I wear her down?"

Golden State remains a young and relatively inexperienced team in the greater landscape of the league, but Veronica Burton said the Valkyries do not feel like underdogs. They were unhappy that last year's playoff appearance (a first-round sweep) "ended as quickly as it started," Burton said, so they don't want to give Dallas the opportunity to take away this series.

stories.headline: Fantasy basketball: The pros and cons of points, roto and category leagues
stories.summary: Which fantasy basketball scoring format should you play? Jim McCormick breaks down the most popular options so you can choose for yourself.
stories.body:
They often say in boxing that styles make fights. The idiom suggests that unique approaches and strategies to the same sport can prove compelling. A southpaw slugger against a quick-footed righty adds to the sweetness of the science.

In a fantasy sports context, formats make things more fun.

When it comes to fantasy basketball, some managers are drawn to a season-long balancing act; curating each statistical category to remain competitive in 3-pointers while also making sure to have enough rim protection. Such managers would be ideal for rotisserie (roto) leagues -- or weekly head-to-head category leagues -- where statistical balance across your roster is the ultimate goal.

Others might prefer to compete in something closer to the fantasy football experience; which we call points leagues in fantasy hoops. These leagues lean on a scoring legend that rewards a specific number of points for each stat accumulated (one point for a rebound, four points for a block, for instance). Check out ESPN's default scoring for points leagues to better understand how this format values each category.

With this in mind, we've done some of the work for you; laying out the pros and cons of roto/category and points-driven formats to help refine the process. The good news is that you can also choose to play in each of these unique formats if you participate in multiple leagues.

How do Roto and H2H Category leagues work?
Roto leagues

Using a 10-team roto league as an example, the team that has the most steals by the end of the season earns 10 points, while the least-larcenous team is left with a single point. This is true for each of the categories your league employs.

Each starting roster spot is afforded an 82-game limit, so maximizing games played isn't an applicable angle in the vein that it fuels success in weekly head-to-head competition. That said, you don't want to fall behind too far in games logged, either, as your competition might end up many games ahead once spring arrives.

As for the specific categories your roto or categories league selects, it's advisable to go with a traditional eight-category setup (points, rebounds, steals, blocks, assists, 3-pointers and both field goal and free throw percentages) versus including turnovers, which are ultimately a tax on ball-dominant players. Some possible additions for a ninth category: assist-to-turnover ratio, which considers turnovers but also values efficient distribution and ball-security, or double-doubles, which put more emphasis on bigs who can rebound.

In roto, the team with the highest total of cumulative points in across each category takes home the title. There are no playoffs or late-season upsets to consider, as we must in weekly head-to-head leagues. This does not mean the format isn't exciting or compelling; roto merely demands a season-long grind from managers. Finally catching your friend in steals thanks to an awesome surge of swipes from Marcus Smart in early April is undeniably rewarding.

H2H Category leagues

Another fun format, head-to-head category leagues, stems from the old-school energy of rotisserie, but is a bit more modernized in that teams compete each week. My home league, for instance, competes head-to-head weekly just like a fantasy football format might, but we use the nine categories noted in the prior paragraph. So, for instance, a dominant week might see you go 7-2 across said categories, while many weeks the margins are 5-4 or 6-3. The top records head to the playoffs come spring.

In these two formats, we covet players who can contribute a consistently diverse collection of statistics, as each category is weighted equally in regards to points. Which is to say, you don't get more points for leading your roto league in points than you do for pacing the competition in steals -- it simply all matters in this format.

The Pros of Roto and Category Leagues

Nuance and balance drive success. Basketball is a sport that counts so many meaningful statistics, while football is largely centered around touchdowns, receptions, and yardage.
Research with a purpose is rewarded. It takes an ability to recognize which 3-point specialist can also find you steals (i.e., Gary Trent Jr.), or which shot-blockers won't tank your free-throw accuracy (i.e., Brook Lopez or Jaren Jackson Jr.).
In rotisserie leagues, the full season plays out. The volatility of a playoff bracket is removed. The winner is truly the most balanced and well-crafted team. There is some volatility present in head-to-head category leagues, but the balance of leveraging eight-to-nine categories also buffers the upset factors that we find in points leagues.

The Cons of Roto and Category Leagues

It's a grind. In what is a counter to some of the pros above, not all of us want to carefully balance our fantasy rosters. Sometimes, it's just fun to chase volume over nuance.
It's tougher to make a comeback: In a roto league, as the games mount, it becomes more daunting to scale the standings if you've punted (ignored a category) or simple fell victim to lots of injuries. This makes staying enthused into the spring more challenging for some.

How do Points leagues work?
The total points generated by the players on your roster are tallied each week, and you get a win or a loss that week based on whether you outscore your weekly opponent. If this sounds a lot like how weekly fantasy football works, it's because the formats are quite similar. At the end of the regular season, the top grouping of teams makes the playoffs and the final team left through this elimination bracket is champion.

The comparison to football isn't perfect, however, as the NBA season is obviously far longer and there are dozens more games played by each team. In most weeks, your fantasy basketball players will play three or four games rather than the singular outcomes of the NFL.

An extra two months of games helps remove some of the volatility and variance that can make fantasy football feel a bit vexing at times. With the marathon of the NBA, surviving a slow start is much more reasonable (shout out to those 1-4 fantasy football teams still keeping the dream alive). Even more fun is that basketball players have more on-and-off court time to develop over the course of the long season, unlike the sprint and unforgiving nature of the gridiron.

The joy of points leagues is the sheer value volume. Big-time scorers, rebounders, and playmakers drive some amazing point totals. Just imagine how many points a hot-streak from Nikola Jokic or Giannis Antetokounmpo might generate. Consider the elation of having helio-centric playmakers like Luka Doncic or Shai Gilgeous-Alexander driving your team to glory each week.

The Pros of Points Leagues

Volume is fun: Superstars shine brighter in the NBA more than maybe any other pro league. The single-named superstars: Luka, Embiid, "Joker," LeBron, et cetera, are even more celebrated when accumulation is king.
Aligns with our love for fantasy football. Week-by-week, it's about who has more points. The victor simply has more points.
Helps simplify a long season. Some want to have a fun and competitive companion to help augment the NBA marathon. While roto and category leagues are awesome for us spreadsheet warriors, points leagues are more accessible and relatable.

The Cons of Points Leagues

Lack of nuance. Basketball is an analytically-friendly game and points formats can in some ways oversimplify outcomes.
Volatility and variance: Many of us have had elite, once-in-a-decade fantasy basketball or football rosters felled by a single bad week in the fantasy playoffs. Such results are still natural in head-to-head points league in hoops.

What's right for you?
Recognizing that we have choices is empowering. Part of this power comes from being able to research and realize which type of fantasy league is best for us and our friends that we compete with throughout the NBA season.

stories.headline: Ayrton Senna's Honda NSX could fetch £800,000 at London auction
stories.summary: A 1991 Honda NSX that once belonged to Ayrton Senna will go up for auction in London at the end of October.
stories.body:
A 1991 Honda NSX that once belonged to Ayrton Senna will go up for auction in London at the end of October.

Chassis number T000233 was one of three NSXs delivered to Senna as part of his contract with Honda in the early 1990s and, due to its provenance, carries an estimate of £500,000 to £800,000.

When the car first went on sale in 1990 it had a list price of between £52,000 and £55,000, with low-mileage NSXs from the same era currently listed online for up to £135,000.

The legendary Japanese sports car is closely linked to Senna, who contributed to its development before it went on sale as Honda's answer to the more expensive Porsche and Ferrari sportscars of the era.

Chassis T000233 is finished in Formula Red over a black leather interior and was delivered to Portugal in March 1991 so that Senna could make use of it while staying at his property in Quinta do Lago.

According to the listing on Sotheby's website, the NSX featured in the 1992 documentary, 'Ayrton Senna: Racing Is In My Blood' and was used by the Brazilian to commute to the 1991 Portuguese Grand Prix in Estoril.

Senna, who died in an accident at the 1994 San Marino Grand Prix, won all three of his world titles with Honda power while racing at McLaren.

stories.headline: Former draftee slams AFL over concussion plight
stories.summary: An AFL draftee whose life was upended by a concussion injury says he "was so close to ending everything".
stories.body:
An AFL draftee whose life was upended by a concussion injury says he "was so close to ending everything".

Aiden O'Driscoll, who had to retire because of a devastating training injury without making his AFL debut, also slammed the league as an "absolute joke".

"The last couple of years I've experienced nothing but pain, and I've explained it multiple times to you. You're supposed to help AFL players through hardship, not leave them with absolutely nothing," O'Driscoll wrote in his extensive Instagram post.

His comments came a day after Geelong announced defender Jake Kolodjashnij had retired.

Last month, the Cats were fined $140,000 and current AFL chairman Craig Drummond apologised after it emerged the club had agreed to a secret concussion waiver with Kolodjashnij. Drummond was Geelong president at the time the agreement was struck.

The Geelong controversy highlighted the complexity and sensitivity around contact sport's concussion crisis.

The Western Bulldogs recruited O'Driscoll in the 2023 draft. But a head injury that summer left him with significant ongoing health problems and the club announced in May, 2024 that he had retired on medical grounds.

"The doctors described my concussion as 'one of the worst' they've seen, with eight micro brain bleeds, and (a) fracture behind my ear," O'Driscoll wrote.

"From a medical point of view, losing my career, my identity plus going through the symptoms I have, you'd think the AFL would be useful with some support?

O'Driscoll added it took the AFL six weeks to find him a psychologist.

"Through this period, I was grieving the most, it got to the point where I started questioning my life? If it was worth living?," he wrote.

"I was so close to ending everything, I would've been free from all the pain/trauma. My family/close friends and partners honestly kept me here."

Melbourne premiership player Angus Brayshaw also had to retire in 2024 because of his concussion issues.

In his emotional toast to other retiring players at the Brownlow Medal function that year, Brayshaw referred to O'Driscoll by name.

"I know a few other past players that are dealing with the same issues as I am," O'Driscoll said.

"AFL it's time to step up! I'm a 21-year-old that can't keep suffering each week. While you're at it, help the other past players that need support."

O'Driscoll added he had been told at 18 never to play contact sport again.

The AFL and the players' association were contacted for comment.

stories.summary: Here's a look at every weight class to determine the best of the best in UFC, PFL and beyond.

stories.headline: Cleary completes golden set with Dally M triumph
stories.summary: Nathan Cleary has completed rugby league's boxed set, with the Penrith star claiming his maiden Dally M Medal after romping to a dominant victory at the NRL's gala night.
stories.body:
Nathan Cleary has completed rugby league's boxed set, with the Penrith star claiming his maiden Dally M Medal after romping to a dominant victory at the NRL's gala night.

Unable to attend the awards after his horror ankle injury in Penrith's preliminary-finals loss, Cleary finished 14 points clear of Cronulla half Braydon Trindall.

Tamika Upton also claimed her third Dally M Medal as NRLW player of the year, defending her crown from last year when the Brisbane fullback became the award's first multiple winner.

Warriors mentor Andrew Webster pipped Justin Holbrook to be the NRL's coach of the year, while Canberra playmaker Ethan Sanders was rookie of the year.

But the story of the night was Cleary, who left hospital on Wednesday after undergoing emergency surgery on his ankle.

Despite being the best player of this decade, the Dally M had somehow evaded Cleary due to a run of injuries or suspensions.

But he played 23 games this year, setting up 29 tries and acting as the chief architect of Penrith's run to the preliminary final.

Cleary, 28, led the race for the majority of the year, polling 67 votes ahead of Trindall's 53 and Panther Dylan Edwards' 52.

Haumole Olakau'atu finished fourth, while Herbie Farnworth and Scott Drinkwater tied for fifth at the gala night at Sydney's Barangaroo.

Cleary had earlier this year claimed his maiden Wally Lewis Medal, silencing his critics by leading NSW to a 2-1 State of Origin series victory.

He has also won two Clive Churchill Medals to go with his four premierships at Penrith.

Meanwhile, Newcastle's magical run to the grand final was not reflected in the Dally M team of the year, with the Knights having no players in the side.

Kalyn Ponga also missed out on captain of the year and Holbrook as coach, with all voting complete at the end of the regular season, when the Knights finished seventh.

Robert Toia and Naufahu Whyte were the two Sydney Roosters representatives named in the side.

In the NRLW, Upton's win came after she polled six points in the penultimate round and then one point in Round 11 to beat Wests Tigers' half Raecene McGregor.

Newcastle winger Mercedez Taulelei-Siala was named rookie of the year, after a season when she scored 13 tries in 12 games. Gold Coast mentor Karyn Murphy won the coach's medal.

The heart-touching moment of the night came when South Sydney's Jai Arrow was presented the Peter Frilingos headline moment and the Provan-Summons spirit of the game award for the way he has approached his battle with motor neurone disease.

stories.headline: Fantasy football matchup rankings: Upgrade Tyler Warren, Tetairoa McMillan in Week 4
stories.summary: The most and least favorable matchups in the NFL for this week's games at the four key fantasy positions.
stories.body:
Making tough lineup decisions each week can be the most challenging part of fantasy football. When you're torn between two similar players, start the player with the superior matchup.

But exactly how does one determine the best (and worst) weekly matchups?

The matchup rankings provide a schedule-independent method to evaluate positional matchups, ranking all 32 opposing defenses in order of most to least favorable for opposing players at all four skill positions. Instead of relying upon seasonal totals, we calibrate points-allowed data to show how each defense fared relative to the difficulty of the schedule it has faced.

For Week 4, 2026 full-season data is used, but once five weeks are in the books, only the most recent five weeks' numbers will be used.

"Adj. FPA," or Adjusted Fantasy Points Allowed, reflects how far above or below players' weekly PPR fantasy point averages that defense held opponents at that position. A positive number means that the matchup is favorable; a negative number means it is unfavorable.

Finally, a caveat: Matchups are only one ingredient in my rankings formula. Not every favorable matchup should be exploited, nor unfavorable matchup avoided. If you want the most complete source for whom to start, consult our weekly rankings.

Quarterbacks

Matchups highlight: Jared Goff, Detroit Lions (at Carolina Panthers, "Sunday Night Football"). One the more quietly reliable quarterbacks, Goff joins Josh Allen, Brock Purdy and Tyler Shough among four with at least 16 fantasy points in each of the season's first three weeks. Of those four, he's the only one who hasn't been intercepted. Goff next faces the Panthers defense, which, aside from their 24-point Week 2 against the Atlanta Falcons third- and fourth-string quarterbacks, has been beaten up by the position. Caleb Williams (Week 1) and Deshaun Watson (Week 3) combined averaged 0.59 fantasy points per passing attempt -- the league average is 0.45 -- against the Panthers.

Others to like:

Trevor Lawrence, Jacksonville Jaguars (at Cincinnati Bengals)

Bryce Young, Panthers (at Lions, SNF)

Matchup to avoid: Jalen Hurts, Philadelphia Eagles (vs. Los Angeles Rams). He's off to a so-so start despite facing a favorable September schedule (WSH, @TEN, @CHI), due to inconsistent protection -- the Eagles rank 22nd in pass block win rate -- and a running game that hasn't fully launched (13th-ranked 110.7 yards per game, 19th-ranked 9.2% explosive run rate). That's of concern when Hurts faces the Rams, who rank second in yards allowed per passing attempt (5.2) and ninth in Total QBR allowed (53.2). Hurts' mobility presents his best case for a top-10 positional ranking this week, but aim to do better from that lineup slot.

Running backs

Matchups highlight: Aaron Jones Sr., Minnesota Vikings (vs. Miami Dolphins). Game script could be a big factor here, which is why Jones gets the nod despite pedestrian 3.9 yards per carry and 11.6 fantasy points per game averages. The Vikings are favored by 11.5, but the game has an over/under of 38.5. Over the past three years, there have been only nine teams favored by more than 10 with a sub-40 over/under. In those games, all nine won and their primary running backs averaged 14.8 fantasy points, 16.2 carries and 18.9 touches. Jones' 67% snap and 61% carry shares suggest he'll capitalize with fantasy RB2 caliber numbers.

Others to like:

David Montgomery, Houston Texans (vs. Dallas Cowboys)

D'Andre Swift, Chicago Bears (vs. New York Jets)

Matchup to avoid: Javonte Williams, Cowboys (at Texans). If there's a bright spot to the Texans' awful showing through three weeks, it's their run defense. The Texans have faced three of the first 16 picks in average ESPN drafts -- James Cook III (Week 1), Chase Brown (Week 2) and Jonathan Taylor (Week 3) -- and limited them to 3.7 yards per carry, an 8.9% explosive run rate and a 10.1 fantasy point average. Even in his breakthrough 2025, Williams delivered ordinary numbers when facing tough matchups, averaging 14.2 fantasy points in his five toughest assignments, so temper your expectations here.

Wide receivers

Matchups highlight: Tetairoa McMillan, Panthers (vs. Lions). He's coming off a brutal day against the Cleveland Browns, and largely CB Denzel Ward, in which he ran 45 routes yet garnered only five targets and 3.7 fantasy points. McMillan should find more open space against the Lions' secondary, which has already seen five different wide receivers score 11-plus fantasy points and afforded the position a fourth-best 2.05 points per target. CB D.J. Reed in particular has struggled, surrendering 39.4 fantasy points on eight targets in his 34 head-to-head matchups thus far, and he'll most likely match up frequently with McMillan.

Others to like:

Josh Downs, Indianapolis Colts (at Washington Commanders, Sunday 9:30 a.m. ET in London)

Michael Wilson, Arizona Cardinals (at New York Giants)

Tee Higgins, Bengals (vs. Jaguars)

Matchup to avoid: DJ Moore, Buffalo Bills (vs. New England Patriots). He returned from a shoulder injury to post a 38% target share and 12.7 fantasy point stat line against the Los Angeles Chargers in Week 3, but Moore has a much tougher assignment in the Patriots this week. Though CB Christian Gonzalez doesn't typically shadow the opponent's No. 1 wideout, and didn't in either of these teams' matchups in 2025, he's likely to see his most head-to-head matchups with Moore. Sure, Jaxon Smith-Njigba had a big score against the Patriots in Week 1 (26.2 fantasy points), but even with that score, Gonzalez and the Patriots rank 18th in fantasy points allowed per target to the position, and 20th in points per target to No. 1 wideouts.

Tight ends

Matchups highlight: Tyler Warren, Colts (at Commanders). He's averaging a serviceable 13.1 fantasy points per game, seventh best at the position, but Daniel Jones' inability to get anything done in the deep game has lowered Warren's ceiling (at least until Alec Pierce heals). Warren's 1.9 yard average depth of target is nearly four yards shorter than he had in 2025, but at least he should be able to rack up yards after the catch. The Commanders have afforded 20-plus fantasy points to tight ends in each of their first three games, have allowed the most points per target to the position (3.21) and have served up the second-highest yards after the catch average to tight ends (8.9).

Matchup to avoid: Mark Andrews, Baltimore Ravens (vs. Tennessee Titans). Between the healthy return of Zay Flowers and Andrews' own hand injury, which limited him to only 47% of the offensive snaps, the veteran tight end scored a season-low 5.4 fantasy points in Week 3. Things don't seem likely to improve this week, against a Titans defense that has been excellent against the position. Facing Kenyon Sadiq (Week 1), Dallas Goedert (Week 2, though shortened due to injury) and Isaiah Likely (Week 3), the Titans afforded the trio a combined 16.1 fantasy points, and 6.3 of those came on a Sadiq end-around rush.

stories.headline: Pep Guardiola after Man City guilty verdict: 'I am behind my club'
stories.summary: Pep Guardiola has released his first statement since Manchester City were found guilty of over 100 breaches of Premier League financial rules, saying "I am behind my club."
stories.body:
Pep Guardiola has released his first statement since Manchester City were found guilty of over 100 breaches of Premier League financial rules, saying "I am behind my club."

Guardiola released a picture of himself alongside City chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak and a full statement on Wednesday which read: "I want every single Manchester City fan across the world to know I am here; more than ever. I am, always have been, always will, be behind my club, my owner, my chairman, Ferran, the players, staff, Enzo and you, our unique supporters.

"Let me be clear: we will get through this together. I love you all."

Guardiola left City in the summer after more than a decade in their dugout, having won 20 trophies. He was replaced by Enzo Maresca who has started strongly, with City currently topping the Premier League.

The club were hit with guilty verdicts from an independent commission relating to their "serious breaches of the Premier League's financial rules" on Friday. They intend to appeal before the deadline on Friday Oct. 2.

Jamie Carragher has called for City to be stripped of the titles won under Guardiola's management during the period that relates to the guilty verdicts.

Supporters' group The Citizens Trust had earlier issued a statement which read: "The Citizens Trust has read both the Premier League's statement on the verdict which finds Manchester City guilty of the majority of the charges, and the club's statement in rebuttal that reiterates their innocence and intent to appeal.

"We are still digesting the full findings of the independent commission, released by the PL in redcated format, and we encourage Blues to do the same.

- Does Man City's guilty verdict impact Pep Guardiola's legacy as an all-time coaching great?

- Ex-Man City chairman calls for club's directors to resign after Premier League guilty verdict

- Roy Keane: I'd put Man City medals 'in the bin' after 'cheating'

"Within an hour of the verdict dropping, we had an emergency meeting with the Football Supporters' Association to assist us as we begin to consider our next steps and what this means for the Trust, the City fanbase and our club going forwar as we await fnal outcomes of any sanctions and appeal.

"We will also be engaging with our members and the winder fanbase as soon as possible. This means consulting the membership, gauging opinion and holding an accessible meeting in Manchester city centre in the near future.

"We all need to look out for each other as supporters in these uncertain times ahead. We need to be strong, together."

Other NHL rivalries remain razor-hot regardless of the standings, and that's the case with the Battle of Pennsylvania between the Pittsburgh Penguins and Philadelphia Flyers.

Both clubs were part of the NHL's 1967 expansion, and have been geographic rivals since.
